items.title: AI is Better Than You at Your Own Job
items.summary: Companies want humans to check the AI. They may be cutting the exact practice that teaches people how. This one is about how new people learn on the job. A lot of it happens in the annoying review meeting, when your manager asks why you picked those numbers. If AI makes the forecast and nobody asks, the work still gets done, but you may miss the practice. I think AI could help you learn faster if someone still makes you explain your choices and check the result. That takes time, and a company might be tempted to cut it.

items.title: From AI Slop to Software Factories ft. Dexter Horthy
items.summary: Two people, one tandem bike, and a lot of near misses along Amsterdam’s canals. Dexter Horthy, CEO and co-founder of HumanLayer and the person who coined “context engineering,” climbs on the back to talk about a problem every AI-heavy engineering team eventually hits: code that runs today that nobody understands three months later. The ride starts with an old joke from the Claude 3.7 days: ship the slop, it’ll be GPT 7’s problem. That joke is aging badly now that GPT 6 is out and still can’t design clean abstractions. From there it becomes a tour of how agents are actually used right now. Computer use checks in for flights and books government appointments. Two hours of raw footage became a rough but promising product demo through Opus 4.8 and the Palmier MCP while Dex was out for a run. And the best MCP tools turn out to be the ones that mirror what Claude Code and Codex were trained to call. Off the bike, over pour-over coffee, the questions get bigger. Are browser agents a bandaid until everything goes headless? What happens to ad-funded websites and upsells when an agent does the shopping? Why does chat still feel like such a low-bandwidth way to work with models? And why is every principal engineer quietly building their own software factory, then getting buried in the sync, streaming and approval plumbing that HumanLayer wants to turn into building blocks, the way GitHub Actions did for CI? items.title: A New Transformer for TEMPORAL Attention #ai
items.summary: A new temporal causal reasoning former (TCR-Former) with a modified temporal attention mechanism. Note: One of the new elements is a separate "event slot", or multiples of them (128). An event slot is a learned numerical representation of a potential event from the text itself, not the event itself, not a timestamp alone, and not a causal rule. Its sole purpose is to gather event information into a form that can be temporally supervised and supplied to the decoder. Another way to see it is that each event slot is kind of an additional feature vector for temporal causal reasoning. Its intended purpose is to collect information about one potential event from the document and provide that information to the reasoning decoder. The earlier "event slots" cannot directly read the later slots. This is the intended connection between the ordered slots and temporal reasoning: later event representations can build on earlier representations. The linear sequence of those event slots provides an ordered scaffold for temporal representations. The authors intend the model to learn a correspondence between position in the event-slot sequence and the temporal organization of events. That ordering is an important part That ordering is an important part, but the main "temporal learning" is happening on the complex encoder-projector-decoder system. The model receives ordered event–timestamp supervision, and the "timestamp head" (see video) encourages slot representations to predict (!) the associated event times. So we have: ordered event slots + directional attention + temporal supervision. all rights w/ authors: From Document Layout to Causal Topology: An End-to-End Architecture for Temporal Causal Reasoning Zhifeng Yang1, Wei Luo1, Yongjian Chen1, Shiqi Ou1,2† from 1 School of Future Technology, South China University of Technology 2 Guangdong Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy Laboratory (Guangzhou) #airesearch #ainnovation #aitech

items.title: Text-to-speech prompting tips
items.summary: How to prompt a text-to-speech model for voice agents: hyphens for stutters, ellipses for pauses, capitals and punctuation for emphasis, and how AssemblyAI TTS reads currency, email addresses, dates, abbreviations and phone numbers. Every tip is tested live in the AssemblyAI playground. The full prompting guide, as a markdown file you can hand to your agent: https://www.assemblyai.com/docs/tts/prompting-guide.md?utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tts-prompting-tips&utm_source=youtube Try our API for free → https://www.assemblyai.com/dashboard/signup?utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=tts-prompting-tips&utm_source=youtube Pacing and tone come from how you write the text. Hyphens make a voice stutter over a word, three dots add a pause (where you put them matters), and capitals, exclamation marks and questions change what the voice emphasizes and how a sentence ends. Filler words are written out, and two letters are enough: "hm" comes out as "hmm". A word followed by a hyphen and a space gives you a false start. Voice agents spend most of their time reading out numbers, addresses and confirmation codes, so the second half covers normalization: a dollar sign makes an amount read as dollars, email addresses are read out as addresses, a date written in numbers is read month first (even 24/10/2026 came out as October 24th), "St" is read as "Street", and common abbreviations like USA and MIT are read as expected. For a less common acronym, put hyphens between the letters. And for numbers, hyphens group the digits, while a comma makes "4,321" read as a whole number. items.title: HCLTech just launched AI-powered nano GCCs on AWS
items.summary: Getting an AI demonstration to work is easy, but getting it to reliably handle everyday business operations is a massive challenge. To bridge this gap, HCLTech has launched an AI-powered nano Global Capability Centre (GCC) offering, built directly on Amazon Web Services (AWS). Instead of launching massive hubs, these nano centres focus on small, highly targeted teams to solve specific business problems before expanding gradually. The target market: Existing GCCs and mid-sized companies looking to introduce AI with delivery anchored from HCLTech's Lucknow centre. The practical gap: Moving from a simple AI trial to sorting thousands of customer messages, checking mistakes, and protecting data. items.title: AI Detectors Are Failing Innocent Students
items.summary: In episode 1039 of the SuperDataScience Podcast, Jon Krohn talks with Dr. John Renne about why AI detectors are failing students. Dr. Renne explains that detectors are notoriously bad and easy to evade, that students wrongly accused of using AI have sued their universities, and how a false positive rate of four to five percent turns into hundreds or even thousands of disputed papers a year at a university with 30,000 students.
